title: karma: a service capstone — a year designed and reviewed
hook: a blank summer calendar, and a verse that says the squares fill anyway
carry: karma: a service capstone — a year designed and reviewed
tomorrow: who is a year of service really for? the circle is wider.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the chakras as a map came home: up to a meeting at the crown, then back down the same road. That closed the Tantras. Today a new stretch begins: karma, and a year of service.

A blank calendar for the summer, every square empty. It looks like freedom, all that open space, and maybe a little like pressure: shouldn't some of those squares do some good? The Bhagavad Gita has a blunt reply to the empty-calendar feeling. Nobody, it says, stays even a moment without acting. The squares will fill. So, one question for today: where does a year of service start?
screen: `A BLANK SUMMER CALENDAR.` → `THE SQUARES WILL FILL.` → `WHERE DOES SERVICE START?`

segments.voice: This week is a capstone, the stone set on top that holds the wall below together. The path of action, karma, turns practical here: design a year of service, and a way to review it. First, the ground it stands on. In chapter three, Krishna says no one can remain even for a moment without acting; the strands of nature move everyone to act. So karma, action, isn't a hobby a person takes up. Then he adds: do the work that's yours to do; action is better than no action, and even keeping the body alive takes action. That gives the first design rule, and it's a surprising one. A year of service doesn't start with a grand new project. It starts with the work already on the calendar: the job, the meals, the care of a parent, the ride to school. Now a neighbor. In the Hebrew Bible, the book of Ecclesiastes puts it this way in the King James Version: "Whatsoever thy hand findeth to do, do it with thy might." The same starting place: what's already in your hand. Here's the honest difference. Ecclesiastes gives its reason right after: in the grave there is no work, so act while you can. Krishna's reason is that no one can step out of acting at all, and he asks for the work to be done without clinging to its fruits. One urges because time runs out. The other, because action never stops.
screen: `NO ONE STAYS A MOMENT WITHOUT ACTING.` · `START WITH THE WORK ALREADY YOURS.` · `ECCLESIASTES: WHAT THY HAND FINDETH.` · `TWO REASONS: TIME, AND ACTION ITSELF.` · then, large: `START WITH WHAT'S IN YOUR HANDS.`

segments.voice: Picture your week, square by square. Count on your fingers the things you already do that serve someone: a meal made, a ride given, a message answered, a shift worked. Let each one land with a breath, as if it were already part of the plan, because it is.
Karma: action, which no one can step out of. In the Gita, a year of service starts with the work already in your hands.
Your line: karma, a service capstone, a year designed and reviewed. It starts with what's already on the calendar. See you in the morning.

howItsDone: Some Hindus read the Bhagavad Gita's third chapter as a call to do one's own daily work as an offering, without clinging to results; service, seva, can be woven into ordinary family and work life.

chat.meaning: Both start with the work at hand: Ecclesiastes because life is short, Krishna because no one can avoid acting.

Unity thread (wisdom day): Ecclesiastes 9:10, KJV, quoted exactly ('Whatsoever thy hand findeth to do, do it with thy might'); the rest of the verse (no work in the grave) is paraphrased.
